phishing-anatomy.brief: An invoice from a supplier has just arrived. Before anyone pays it, investigate it in Mail: find three red flags, then report it. Look closely without opening anything.

objectives.link: The link hides its real destination
objectives.attachment: The attachment is a program in disguise
objectives.report: Report the email with Report phishing

why.sender: View original shows SPF, DKIM and DMARC all failing: the message did not come from the supplier's mail servers. The Reply-To points to another domain, so any answer would go to someone else.
why.link: The link text shows the supplier's portal, but the status bar reveals a different domain. Always check where a link really goes before you click it.
why.attachment: The file name hides “.exe” after many spaces, so it looks like a PDF. A program sent as an invoice is a classic way to get malware onto a computer.
why.report: Reporting lets the security team block the sender and warn colleagues who got the same email. One report can protect the whole company.

ruleWhy.noAttachment: Opening an unexpected attachment can run malware immediately. Check its details instead, and report the email.
ruleWhy.noLink: Following the link takes you to a page made to collect your sign-in or start a download. Inspect links, don't click them.

hints.h1: Real senders pass the mail server's checks. Open the email and choose View original.
hints.h2: Hover over the link (or select it with Tab) and read the status bar at the bottom of the window.
hints.h3: Open the attachment's details with the ⓘ button next to it and read the full file name.

phishing-anatomy.falseReport: You also reported a genuine email. Reporting when unsure is always fine, but look for evidence first.

process-hunt.brief: The security team saw WS-114 contacting an unknown server every minute. Investigate in the Terminal: find the program, check the address, stop it and remove it from startup. Leave legitimate software alone.
process-hunt.welcome: Lumen Freight workstation WS-114. Type help to see the commands. Your ticket is in ~/notes.
process-hunt.ticket:
TICKET SEC-2291 · priority: high
WS-114 contacts an unknown external IP address every 60 seconds.
The user installed a free PDF tool yesterday.
Please: find the process, check the IP, stop the process
and make sure it does not start again at the next login.
Nimbus Sync and Lumen VPN are approved company software.

objectives.find: Find the process talking to an unknown external IP

why.find: netstat -an lists every connection with the program behind it. sysupd keeps reconnecting to 203.0.113.77, while the other external connections belong to approved software.
why.whois: whois shows who owns an address. 203.0.113.77 belongs to an anonymous hosting service registered three days ago, unlike the company's known cloud and VPN providers. Checking before acting avoids stopping the wrong thing.
why.kill: Stopping the process (kill 4242) cuts the connection at once, so the program can no longer send data out or receive commands.
why.persist: Unwanted programs add themselves to startup so they come back after a restart. Removing the entry (startup remove sysupd) makes the clean-up last.

ruleWhy.keepProcesses: You stopped approved software. In a real incident that interrupts people's work and can destroy evidence, so check with whois and the ticket first.
ruleWhy.keepStartup: You removed an approved program from startup. Change only what the evidence points to.

hints.h1: Start with netstat -an: look for a foreign address that doesn't belong to the company's approved software.
hints.h2: Run whois with that IP address, then compare it with the PID shown by netstat or ps.
hints.h3: kill with the PID stops the process; startup list shows what starts at login, and startup remove followed by an entry's name removes it.

notes.comeback: You stopped the process but left its startup entry: it would have come back at the next login.
notes.stillRunning: You removed the startup entry but the process was still running and connected.

whois.descr: Kestrel VPS - anonymous virtual servers, crypto payments only
whois.remarks: No customer verification. Reported for malware command-and-control.

fake-signin.brief: A colleague's shared file opened a Cloudora sign-in page. Before you sign in, check it in the Browser: inspect the address and the certificate, then close the tab and report the page. Don't type a password.

why.url: The address looks like cloudora.example, but its second letter is a Cyrillic “о”. The real address is xn--cludora-bjg.example: a different domain registered to look the same.
why.cert: The certificate is issued to files-share-cdn.example with no organisation, by a free certificate service, two days ago. Cloudora's real certificate names cloudora.example and Cloudora Ltd.
why.close: Closing the tab ends the risk: nothing you type there can be sent anymore.
why.report: Reporting lets the security team block the look-alike domain for everyone and warn colleagues who got the same link.

rules.noPassword: Don't type a password on this page

ruleWhy.noPassword: A page like this sends what you type to someone else as you type it. If you ever enter a password on a suspicious page, change it at once and tell the security team.
ruleWhy.noSubmit: Pressing Sign in sends the form. A “wrong password” message afterwards is a common trick to make you type it again.

hints.h1: Click the address in the address bar to see how the computer really reads it.
hints.h2: Click the padlock, then Show certificate: whose name is on it?
hints.h3: Use Report unsafe site in the toolbar (or Report phishing on the email), then close the tab with ×.

faqItems.q: Why do I get phishing emails from my own organisation?
faqItems.a: They are safe training simulations. If you spot one, report it: you earn XP and your department climbs the league.

faqItems.q: What happens if I click a simulation link?
faqItems.a: Nothing bad. You see a short explanation and a training that closes the gap. Your risk score goes down when you finish it.

faqItems.q: Is my data sent to AI Sel?
faqItems.a: No. AI Sel only gets the lesson context and an anonymous ID; never your name, email or job title.

faqItems.q: How is my risk score calculated?
faqItems.a: From unfinished assigned training, simulation results, open risks and first-try answers. My security shows each part.

faqItems.q: Can I learn on my phone?
faqItems.a: Yes. Open the portal in your phone's browser and add it to the home screen.
